[]{#glossary.html}

### []{#glossary.html_anchor_2082_0}[GLOSSARY]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:15px;"}
:::

[Achaemenid:]{.style_1} [The Persian royal house from the region near Persepolis. All Persian kings claimed descent from the supposed founder of the line, Achaemenes. The term is used interchangeably for the royal line of kings and the empire itself.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Achilles:]{.style_1} [Greatest Greek hero of the Trojan War. Alexander claimed ancestry from him through his mother and emulated him in his quest for undying fame.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Ada:]{.style_1} [Satrap of Caria until removed by her brother Pixodarus. She was restored to power by Alexander and adopted him as her son.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Agis:]{.style_1} [King of Sparta and devoted foe of Alexander. Tried to reassert Spartan power in Greece in a coalition against Macedonian rule, but was killed in battle against Antipater at Megalopolis in 331.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Ai Khanum:]{.style_1} [Possibly a colony founded by Alexander, this Bactrian Greek city on the banks of the Oxus (Amu Darya) in northern Afghanistan was excavated by the French, who unearthed evidence of a thriving settlement that survived until the mid-second century B.C.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Alexander IV:]{.style_1} [Son of Alexander by Roxane. He was used as a pawn in the wars of succession and killed along with his mother in 310.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Alexander of Epirus:]{.style_1} [Brother of Olympias and king of Epirus. His ties to Macedonia were strengthened when he married Philip's daughter, Cleopatra. He died fighting in Italy in 331.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2097_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Alexandria]{.style_1} [(Egypt): Founded by Alexander in 331 on the Mediterranean coast near the westernmost edge of the Nile delta. Ptolemy built a tomb for Alexander here after hijacking his body on its journey back to Macedonia. The city grew to be a major center of Hellenistic civilization with more than a million inhabitants, including a large Jewish community. It was famed for the Pharos lighthouse, museum, and library.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Alexandria:]{.style_1} [The name given to a number of cities founded by Alexander from the Mediterranean to India.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Ammon:]{.style_1} [The major Egyptian god Amun identified by Greeks with Zeus. His oracle at the oasis of Siwa on the modern border between Egypt and Libya was visited by Alexander in 331.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Antigonus:]{.style_1} [A Macedonian nobleman known as Monophthalmus ("one-eyed"), who was a contemporary of Philip's. Alexander appointed him satrap of Phrygia in Asia Minor. He was a major player in the wars of succession after Alexander's death.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Antipater:]{.style_1} [Trusted Macedonian nobleman and lieutenant under Philip. Alexander appointed him regent of Macedonia and Greece while he campaigned in Asia. He defeated Agis of Sparta when he revolted, but later fell from favor and faced replacement by Craterus. An important figure in the struggle for power after the death of Alexander.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Arabia:]{.style_1} [The modern Arabian peninsula that in ancient times was a major source of incense and spices. Alexander was preparing to conquer it when he died in Babylon in 323.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Aristander:]{.style_1} [An influential seer from Telmessus in Lycia skilled at interpreting omens to favor Alexander.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Aristobulus:]{.style_1} [An engineer and architect who accompanied Alexander on his expedition. In his old age, he wrote a flattering account of Alexander that was a major source for Arrian.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2113_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Aristotle:]{.style_1} [Student of Plato, tutor of Alexander, and one of the most influential and learned thinkers of ancient times. Born in Stagira in northern Greece in 384, he was the son of the court physician to Alexander's grandfather, King Amyntas III. He spent part of his childhood at the Macedonian court at Pella. He taught Alexander and his young companions at Mieza in Macedonia and maintained contact with his royal pupil throughout his campaigns, receiving scientific specimens from many parts of Asia.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Arrhidaeus:]{.style_1} [Half brother of Alexander and son of Philip II by one of his seven wives, Philinna of Thessaly. Reportedly mentally impaired, he was unexpectedly proclaimed king at Babylon in 323 along with Alexander's infant son. He was a pawn in the hands of the successors and was later murdered by Olympias.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Arrian:]{.style_1} [Most influential ancient biographer of Alexander, Arrian was born in Bithynia and served the Roman government in important political and military offices in Asia. A student of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus, his]{.style_0} [Anabasis of Alexander]{.style_1} [and]{.style_0} [Indica]{.style_1} [remain key sources for modern biographers of Alexander.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Artabazus:]{.style_1} [Persian nobleman who revolted against the empire and fled to the Macedonian court in 352. He later returned to Persia and was loyal to Darius until the king's murder. He then joined Alexander and was appointed satrap of Bactria. His daughter Barsine married Memnon and had a long affair with Alexander that produced a son.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Artaxerxes III:]{.style_1} [Also known as Ochos, he ruled Persia from 359 to 338. He put down a revolt of satraps in Asia Minor and reconquered Egypt before he was assassinated. Alexander married his daughter in 324 at the mass wedding in Susa.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Artaxerxes IV:]{.style_1} [Son of Artaxerxes III, he ruled Persia from 338 to 336. He was assassinated and followed on the throne by Darius.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2125_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Athens:]{.style_1} [Longtime antagonist of Macedonia, it was one of the major cities of Greece and famed for its naval power.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Attalus:]{.style_1} [Macedonian nobleman and son-in-law of Parmenion. He questioned Alexander's legitimacy as a worthy heir to the throne and was killed soon after Philip's assassination.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Babylon:]{.style_1} [An ancient and celebrated city of Mesopotamia on the Euphrates south of modern Baghdad. It was the capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire and an important city of the Persian Empire. Alexander visited it in 331 and died there in 323.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Bactria:]{.style_1} [Region in central Asia between the Oxus River on the north and the Hindu Kush mountains to the south, it included much of modern Afghanistan. An important Persia satrapy. Alexander faced some of his fiercest resistance here.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Bagoas:]{.style_1} [Not to be confused with the grand vizier of the same name who murdered two Persian kings, this eunuch, noted for his beauty, was the lover of Darius, then Alexander.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Barsine:]{.style_1} [Daughter of Artabazus and widow of Memnon, she had an affair with Alexander that produced a son named Hercules (Heracles).]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Batis:]{.style_1} [Eunuch and governor of Gaza who resisted Alexander's takeover. This so infuriated Alexander that he was dragged behind a chariot around the city walls of Gaza until dead.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Bessus:]{.style_1} [Satrap of Bactria under Darius, he murdered the Great King and assumed the Persian throne to lead resistance to Alexander in the east. He was captured, mutilated, and executed by Alexander.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Brahmins:]{.style_1} [Priestly caste of India, some of whom resisted Alexander and paid with their lives.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2143_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Bucephalas:]{.style_1} [Thessalian stallion with an ox-shaped mark tamed by Alexander as a boy and ridden by him in his conquests across the Persian Empire. He died in India and was honored by Alexander, who named a city after him.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Calanus:]{.style_1} [Indian holy man who accompanied Alexander back to Persepolis. He died there in a spectacular public suicide.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Callisthenes:]{.style_1} [Born in Olynthus, a town destroyed by Philip, he was a nephew of Aristotle and official historian of Alexander's expedition. He fell from favor after he opposed Alexander's]{.style_0} [proskynesis]{.style_1} [policy and was executed for his alleged involvement in the Pages' Conspiracy.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Caria:]{.style_1} [Coastal region of southwest Asia Minor in modern Turkey conquered by Alexander in 334. The chief city was the port of Halicarnassus.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Carthage:]{.style_1} [Phoenician colony and naval power in modern Tunisia founded from Tyre in the early first millennium B.C. It supported Tyre in resisting Alexander and was reportedly on his list for conquest at the time of his death.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Celts:]{.style_1} [A collection of related tribes dominating central Europe at the time of Alexander. Celtic envoys met Alexander on the Danube in 335 and established a treaty of friendship with him.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Chaeronea:]{.style_1} [Town in central Greece where in 338 Philip defeated the Greek forces, including the Sacred Band of Thebes. It was also Alexander's first major battle.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Chares:]{.style_1} [Chamberlain of Alexander from the Greek island of Lesbos who wrote a long and colorful history of court life under the king.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Cilicia:]{.style_1} [Coastal region in southeast Asia Minor near the modern border between Turkey and Syria. Alexander took Tarsus, the chief city of the area, in 333.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2161_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Cleitarchus:]{.style_1} [late-fourth-century B.C. historian of Alexander whose lengthy work was a major source for later historians.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Cleitus the Black:]{.style_1} [Macedonian nobleman and brother of Alexander's nurse. He saved Alexander's life at the Granicus but later criticized him at a drinking party in Samarkand and was killed by the drunken king.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Cleopatra:]{.style_1} [A common female name among the Macedonian nobility. One so named was the full sister of Alexander married to Alexander of Epirus, while another was the niece of Attalus and seventh wife of Philip.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Coenus:]{.style_1} [Noted Macedonian soldier who was the son-in-law of Parmenion. He sided against his brother-in-law Philotas in 330, but spoke up for the troops at the mutiny on the Hyphasis River in 326. He died soon thereafter.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Corinth:]{.style_1} [Strategic Greek city west of Athens that was the setting for Philip's League of Corinth, established after the battle of Chaeronea in 338. It provided nominal independence and a unified voice to member Greek city-states, but was in fact dominated by Macedonia.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Craterus:]{.style_1} [Important commander of Alexander's at Issus, Gaugamela, and in the eastern campaigns. He participated in the removal of Philotas and Parmenion. Alexander sent him back to Greece just before his death to escort decommissioned troops and replace Antipater in Greece.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Curtius Rufus:]{.style_1} [Roman historian of the second century A.D. known in his history of Alexander for his rhetorical flourishes and frequent criticisms of the king.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Cyrene:]{.style_1} [Greek colony on the north coast of Africa west of Egypt in modern Libya. It submitted to Alexander in 331.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Cyrus the Great:]{.style_1} [King who founded the Persian Empire and rose during the mid--sixth century from ruler of a small territory subject to []{#glossary.html_anchor_2178_24}the Median king to master of an empire stretching from central Asia to the Mediterranean.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Danube:]{.style_1} [European river rising in the Alps and emptying into the Black Sea. Alexander crossed it in 335 and subdued the tribes on his northern border before his invasion of Asia.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Darius I:]{.style_1} [Persian nobleman who seized control of the empire in 522 and invaded Greece in 490, only to be defeated by the Athenians at Marathon.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Darius III:]{.style_1} [Became Persian king in 336 after the murder of Artaxerxes IV and fought Alexander at Issus and Gaugamela. He was murdered by Bessus in 330.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Delphi:]{.style_1} [Famous oracle of Apollo in the mountains of central Greece. Alexander visited the holy site soon after becoming king and extracted a favorable prophesy from the priestess of the god.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Demaratus:]{.style_1} [Native of Corinth and veteran of wars in Sicily, he was a friend of Alexander's father who some say bought the famous horse Bucephalas for Alexander. He later accompanied Alexander to Asia and died shortly before the Indian campaign began.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Demosthenes:]{.style_1} [Famed Athenian orator and vociferous opponent of both Philip and Alexander.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Dion:]{.style_1} [Sacred site in southern Macedonia at the foot of Mount Olympus. It was here that Alexander acquired his horse Bucephalas.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Ecbatana:]{.style_1} [Modern Hamadan in western Iran, it was the Median capital and major palace center under the Persian Empire.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Elam:]{.style_1} [An ancient kingdom in the southwest of modern Iran conquered by the Persians. Susa was its largest and most prosperous city.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2197_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Epirus:]{.style_1} [Roughly modern Albania, this mountainous region west of Macedonia was the homeland of Alexander's mother, Olympias.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Gaugamela:]{.style_1} [Near modern Mosul in northern Iraq, it was here in October of 331 that Alexander won his decisive victory over Darius.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Gedrosia:]{.style_1} [Inhospitable desert region in southeastern Iran through which Alexander marched his army on the return from India to Babylon.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Gordian Knot:]{.style_1} [Gordium was the capital of ancient Phrygia in central Asia Minor. A famously difficult knot around the yoke of an ancient wagon was undone here in 333 by Alexander, some say by unloosing and others by slashing through it with his sword.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Granicus:]{.style_1} [Modern Kocabas River in northwest Turkey, where Alexander won his first great battle against the Persians in 334.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Halicarnassus:]{.style_1} [Now Bodrum on the southwestern coast of Turkey, it was an important Greek city of Caria holding the celebrated tomb known as the Mausoleum. Alexander took the city after a difficult siege in 334.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Harpalus:]{.style_1} [Boyhood friend of Alexander's from upper Macedonia who served the king as treasurer. He deserted Alexander before the battle of Issus, but was forgiven and reinstated, only to desert him again in 324 before Alexander returned to Babylon.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Hephaestion:]{.style_1} [Boyhood friend and intimate companion of Alexander who rose to important military commands later in the Asian expedition. When he died suddenly at Ecbatana in 324, Alexander was inconsolable and buried his friend with extravagant honors.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Hercules:]{.style_1} [In Greek, Heracles. This is the name of both the famed divine hero of Greek myth---considered an ancestor by Alexander---and the son of the king by his mistress Barsine.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2215_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Herodotus:]{.style_1} [Greek historian of the fifth century B.C. from Halicarnassus who wrote a colorful history of much of the known world.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Hindu Kush:]{.style_1} [A mountain range stretching from northern Pakistan to northeast Afghanistan with peaks soaring up to 25,000 feet. Alexander crossed the high passes of this range several times during his campaign.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Homer:]{.style_1} [Famed Greek poet of the eighth century B.C. who composed the]{.style_0} [Iliad]{.style_1} [and]{.style_0} [Odyssey.]{.style_1} [Alexander modeled himself on the hero Achilles from the]{.style_0} [Iliad]{.style_1} [and reportedly slept with a copy of the poem under his pillow.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Hydaspes:]{.style_1} [The modern Jhelum River in Pakistan, where Alexander defeated the Indian king Porus in 326.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Hyphasis:]{.style_1} [The modern Beas River in northern India, where a mutiny of his men forced Alexander to turn back from his planned invasion of the Ganges valley.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Hyrcania:]{.style_1} [Region on the southern shore of the Caspian Sea in modern Iran. Alexander conquered the area in 330.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Illyria:]{.style_1} [Roughly the former Yugoslavia, it was an ancient region of the Balkan peninsula north of Epirus and west of Macedonia. Philip gained control over these lands for Macedon, while Alexander confirmed his power there in an early campaign in 335.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[India:]{.style_1} [The ancient name for the lands stretching from the Indus river valley to the East, especially the region of Punjab. For Greeks such as Alexander, the term encompassed the entire subcontinent, including both modern Pakistan and India.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Isocrates:]{.style_1} [Athenian orator and early advocate of a united Greek invasion of Persia.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2233_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Issus:]{.style_1} [Along the coastal border between modern Turkey and Syria, in 333 it was the site of a decisive victory of Alexander over Darius.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Jaxartes:]{.style_1} [Flowing into the Aral Sea, the modern Syr Darya was the northeastern boundary of the Persian Empire and the scene of fierce fighting by Alexander. He founded the city of Alexandria Eschate ("the farthest") on its banks.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Justin:]{.style_1} [A Roman who may have lived in the third century A.D. who wrote an epitome of the now lost history of the rule of Alexander's father Philip by Pompeius Trogus.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Leonidas:]{.style_1} [Severe boyhood tutor of Alexander with a reputation for frugality who once rebuked Alexander for using too much incense at a sacrifice. With this in mind, Alexander sent him plentiful frankincense and myrrh seized during his Asian campaign.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Lydia:]{.style_1} [Region of western Asia Minor near the Aegean coast in modern Turkey famous for its cavalry. Its capital Sardis was a key city of the Persian Empire in the west.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Lysimachus:]{.style_1} [One of Alexander's boyhood tutors. He had a special affection for Homer that he instilled in Alexander from his early years. He was rescued by his former pupil when threatened with death from exposure in the mountains above Tyre. This is also the name of one of Alexander's commanders who ruled Thrace after the king's death.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Macedonia:]{.style_1} [The region of modern Greece north of Mount Olympus bordered in ancient times on the east by Thrace, on the south by Thessaly, and on the west by Epirus and Illyria.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Magi:]{.style_1} [Though their exact function is poorly understood, these religious professionals performed sacred rituals and preserved oral history among the Medes and Persians. In Greek tradition, as in []{#glossary.html_anchor_2248_29}the New Testament nativity story, they were frequently associated with astrology.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Malli:]{.style_1} [A powerful tribe of the Indus River valley. Alexander was almost killed at one of their cities during an assault on its walls.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Marathon:]{.style_1} [Coastal site to the east of Athens where in 490 the Greeks defeated the invading army of the first Great King Darius.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Mazaeus:]{.style_1} [Persian nobleman who served Darius at the battle of Gaugamela, but then quickly switched sides and helped Alexander take over Babylon. Alexander made him satrap of Babylonia, the first Persian he appointed to such a high post.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Medes:]{.style_1} [In Greek thought, Medes were often confused with their cousins the Persians, but they were in fact a separate people from the northern area of modern Iran. Ecbatana was their capital. Cyrus the Great conquered their kingdom and freed the Persian tribes from their control.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Memnon:]{.style_1} [Greek general from the island of Rhodes who served Darius well until his untimely death in 333. He was married to Barsine, daughter of the Persian satrap Artabazus. He fought at the Granicus and held Alexander back at Halicarnassus before eventually withdrawing to continue the war in the Aegean.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Nearchus:]{.style_1} [Boyhood friend of Alexander from Crete. He first served as a satrap in Asia Minor, then as a naval commander on the rivers of India. He led Alexander's fleet back from India to the Tigris, later recording his exploits in a lost text that was a major source for the historian Arrian.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Olympia:]{.style_1} [Town in western Greece where the Olympic games were held every four years.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2263_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Olympias:]{.style_1} [Wife of Philip and mother of Alexander. Born in Epirus, she was brilliant, resourceful, ambitious, and sometimes cruel as she strove to assure Alexander's place on the throne of Macedonia. After Philip's death, she remained in Macedonia, though in close communication with Alexander while he conquered Persia.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Olympus:]{.style_1} [By tradition the seat of the gods, this towering mountain almost ten thousand feet high marked the southern boundary of Macedonia.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Olynthus:]{.style_1} [Greek city on the Chalcidic peninsula to the east of Macedonia destroyed by Philip in 348 after it intrigued with Athens against him. It was the home of Alexander's official historian, Callisthenes.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Onesicritus:]{.style_1} [Greek student of the philosopher Diogenes who served as helmsman for Alexander's fleet. His lost work described India and portrayed Alexander as a philosopher as much as a warrior.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Oxus:]{.style_1} [The modern Amu Darya, which rises on the northern border of Afghanistan and flows into the Aral Sea. It was the northern border of ancient Bactria.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Pages' Conspiracy:]{.style_1} [An alleged murder plot in 327 by the sons of Macedonian nobles who served Alexander as attendants. Callisthenes was falsely accused of conspiring with the pages and executed.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Parmenion:]{.style_1} [Macedonian nobleman and chief general of Philip who also served Alexander. He is frequently portrayed in the ancient sources as overly cautious in contrast to the daring young Alexander. He was killed on Alexander's orders in 330 soon after the execution of his son Philotas.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Pasargadae:]{.style_1} [Royal Persian burial site near Persepolis where the tomb of Cyrus the Great still stands.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2279_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Pausanius:]{.style_1} [A young bodyguard of Philip who murdered him in 336 after reportedly suffering vile abuse at the hands of Philip's companions.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Pella:]{.style_1} [A notable city of Macedonia as revealed by archaeological excavations. It replaced Vergina (ancient Aegae) as administrative capital in the late fifth century B.C.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Perdiccas:]{.style_1} [A common name among Macedonian nobility, Perdiccas, son of Orontes, was a military leader and bodyguard of Alexander's who succeeded Hephaestion as cavalry commander in 324. He was chosen as guardian of Alexander's son by Roxane, but perished in the wars of the successors.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Persepolis:]{.style_1} [A chief residence of the Persian kings in the heartland of ancient Persia near modern Shiraz, Iran. Alexander burned the palace there in 330, but accounts of his motives vary. Excavations have revealed an impressive city with stunning royal reliefs.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Persians:]{.style_1} [A people of Indo-Iranian speech related to the Medes and more distantly to the tribes of northern India. They were originally warlike tribesmen from the region around Persepolis, but through Cyrus and his successors gained control of the largest empire the world had yet known.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Peucestas:]{.style_1} [A Macedonian who saved Alexander's life during an assault on an Indian city of the Malli. He was promoted to bodyguard and eventually satrap. He was one of the few important Macedonians genuinely to embrace Alexander's policy of orientalism.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Philip of Acarnania:]{.style_1} [Greek physician who saved Alexander's life in 333 before the battle at Issus.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Philip II:]{.style_1} [Alexander's father, husband of Olympias, and man chiefly responsible for turning Macedonia from a struggling secondary power into a mighty empire. He was murdered in 336.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2295_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Philotas:]{.style_1} [Oldest son of Parmenion, he was condemned to death by Alexander's order in 330, closely followed by the murder of his father.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Phoenicia:]{.style_1} [Roughly equivalent to modern Lebanon, this coastal land of the cities Tyre and Sidon was the home of the wide-ranging Phoenicians.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Plutarch:]{.style_1} [Born in the mid--first century A.D., a biographer of famous Greeks and Romans who was a favorite source for Shakespeare. Native to Chaeronea in central Greece, he wrote a moralistic account of Alexander that is our only significant source on the king's early life.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Porus:]{.style_1} [King of the Pauravas in the Punjab region of India, Porus was reportedly a brave and honorable king who fought Alexander well at the battle at the Hydaspes River in 326, but was pardoned and reinstated to his throne afterward. He was later murdered by the Macedonian commander at Taxila.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[pothos: A Greek word indicating a deep desire or yearning. It was used by the historian Arrian to describe the motive of many of Alexander's more audacious and questionable actions.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[proskynesis: A Greek word used for religious worship, but applied to varying acts of obeisance performed before the Persian king. Alexander's efforts to incorporate proskynesis into his court ceremonies met heated resistance by the Macedonians.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Ptolemy:]{.style_1} [Childhood friend and trusted military commander of Alexander's on his campaign against the Persians. He later seized Alexander's body and became king of Egypt, founding a dynasty that ended with the celebrated Cleopatra. His lost memoirs on Alexander's expedition were a key source for later historians, especially Arrian.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Punjab:]{.style_1} [Literally "the land of the five rivers" stretching across northern regions of modern Pakistan into India. Alexander campaigned here in 326.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2311_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Roxane:]{.style_1} [Daughter of the Bactrian nobleman Oxyartes. She married Alexander in 327 just before his invasion of India. Her son, Alexander IV, was his father's only legitimate heir. Both she and her son were murdered in 311.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Samarkand:]{.style_1} [Ancient Markanda, the capital of ancient Sogdiana, lies on the old Silk Road in Uzbekistan. It was a center of Alexander's campaigns starting in 329.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Sardis:]{.style_1} [Ancient capital of Lydia in western Asia Minor, it surrendered to Alexander in 334.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[sarissa:]{.style_1} [An iron-tipped wooden spear up to eighteen feet long used with devastating effect by the well-drilled Macedonian infantry.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[satrap:]{.style_1} [A Persian term borrowed by Alexander for the governor of a province.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Scylax:]{.style_1} [Sailor from Caria in Asia Minor who served the first Great King Darius and explored the sea route from India to Egypt.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Seleucus:]{.style_1} [Known later as Nicator ("conqueror"), he served in Alexander's later campaigns and gained control of Babylonia after Alexander's death. He founded a dynasty that for a time ruled much of Alexander's Asian empire.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Semiramis:]{.style_1} [Legendary queen of Babylon who reportedly led an army through the Gedrosian desert, losing almost all her soldiers on the way.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Sisyngambris:]{.style_1} [Mother of Darius captured at Issus, she was reportedly treated with great respect by Alexander and committed suicide in grief after his death.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Siwa:]{.style_1} [A large oasis on the modern border between Libya and Egypt. It was home of the oracle of Ammon, visited by Alexander in 331.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2331_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Sogdiana:]{.style_1} [Ancient region to the north of Bactria that encompasses much of modern Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Alexander campaigned here beginning in 329.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Sparta:]{.style_1} [Greek city renowned for its military prowess. It had faded in power by Alexander's day, but under its king Agis it rose to challenge Macedonian control of southern Greece, only to be soundly defeated by Alexander's regent Antipater.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Spitamenes:]{.style_1} [Nobleman of Sogdiana who led the resistance to Alexander after the death of Bessus. He staged an effective guerrilla war against the Macedonians for more than a year before being captured and executed.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Susa:]{.style_1} [The ancient capital of Elam in what is now southwestern Iran, it was an administrative capital of the Persians. Alexander took the city without bloodshed in 331 and staged a mass wedding here in 324.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Taxila:]{.style_1} [An ancient city in the northern Indus valley near modern Islamabad, Pakistan. Its king was an early ally of Alexander in India.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Thebes:]{.style_1} [Famous city of central Greece defeated and destroyed by Alexander in 335 as a warning to all who would resist him.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Thermopylae:]{.style_1} [Narrow pass in central Greece where the Spartans and their allies held back the entire invading Persian army in 380 before they were killed to a man.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Thessaly:]{.style_1} [Region just to the south of Macedonia famous for its cavalry.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Thrace:]{.style_1} [Land to the east and north of Macedonia inhabited by warlike tribes.]{.style_0}

[]{#glossary.html_anchor_2349_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Triballi:]{.style_1} [Tribe on the Danube defeated by Alexander in 335 during his early campaign in the northern Balkans. They afterward contributed soldiers to his Asian campaign.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[trireme:]{.style_1} [A type of swift and formidable Greek warship propelled by three ranks of rowers with a bronze battering ram in the prow.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Troy:]{.style_1} [City on the Hellespont in northwest Asia Minor that was the scene of the Trojan War of Greek legend. Excavations at its ruins near modern Canakkale in Turkey have revealed a complex site dating back thousands of years before Alexander's visit in 334.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Tyre:]{.style_1} [Ancient Phoenician city, once an offshore island, on the coast of modern Lebanon that was long besieged and finally taken by Alexander in 332.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Vergina:]{.style_1} [Ancient Aegae, this hillside town overlooks the coastal plains of Macedonia. Excavations here have revealed spectacular royal tombs of the Macedonian kings, including the burial place of Philip. It was also at the theater here that Philip was murdered.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[Zoroaster:]{.style_1} [Greek form of the Persian prophet Zarathushtra, who established a religious tradition based on the opposition of the forces of darkness and light, with Ahuramazda as supreme god.]{.style_0}

[]{#notes.html}

The question of Macedonian language and ethnic identity is one of the most contentious topics in classical scholarship, the debate often driven more by modern Balkan nationalism than the small amount of ancient evidence we actually possess. I incline to the argument that Macedonian was a distant dialect of Greek rather than a separate language. In any case, the practical result in the age of Alexander was that the Macedonians considered themselves and were considered by others as non-Greeks.]{.style_0}

[]{#biblio.html}

### []{#biblio.html_anchor_2952_0}[BIBLIOGRAPHY]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:25px;"}
:::

[**ANCIENT SOURCES**]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:2px;"}
:::

[The ancient sources for the life of Alexander are plentiful but problematic. Unlike Julius Caesar, whose firsthand accounts of the war in Gaul and struggle for Rome survive, Alexander wrote nothing himself that has come down to us aside from a few decrees recorded in inscriptions and fragments from a handful of possibly genuine letters quoted by later authors. Thus the search for accurate accounts of Alexander becomes very much like the quest for the historical Jesus or Socrates. As with these two famous figures from antiquity, our knowledge of Alexander is ultimately dependent on records left by those who knew him, whether friends or enemies. However, even the biographies of Alexander written during his lifetime or soon after his death disappeared from Greek and Roman libraries by late antiquity. This leaves us with only secondhand accounts penned by historians in Roman times who had access to these earlier sources.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[None of this means that the search for the historical Alexander is hopeless---far from it. But we do have to be keenly aware of the problems associated with our sources. Even accounts written by those who knew and traveled with Alexander have their own agenda. Some contemporaries despised the Macedonian king and missed no opportunity to denigrate him as a murderous drunkard craving eternal glory at any cost. Others portrayed him as a noble and kindly soul, the paradigm of a just ruler. Like every modern historian, each ancient biographer was deeply influenced by the circumstances in which he wrote and by his own prejudices.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[The ancient sources on Alexander begin with []{#biblio.html_anchor_2960_8}Callisthenes, the nephew of Aristotle and native of the Greek city of Olynthus, a town destroyed by Alexander's father, Philip. Alexander chose Callisthenes to accompany him on his expedition and send back flattering reports of his heroic exploits to the Greeks. Callisthenes undoubtedly harbored much ill will toward the royal house of Macedonia for obliterating his hometown, but he obliged Alexander with obsequious propaganda until the king had him executed. His reports were widely available, at least in part, to most of the ancient biographers of Alexander.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[One of the most important early biographers of Alexander was his boyhood friend Ptolemy, son of Lagus, later the pharaoh of Egypt. Ptolemy was by Alexander's side from the first campaigns on the Danube to the final days in Babylon. As a lifelong companion with intimate knowledge of Alexander's life, he could hardly be a better source---except that Ptolemy had a vested interest in portraying his friend in a positive light. Writing from Alexandria in his later years, he needed a heroic and admirable Alexander to strengthen his own legitimacy as a successor and ruler of Egypt. Even so, Ptolemy was not a sycophant and was a crucial source on the details of Alexander's military conquests for later writers, especially Arrian.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[Another eyewitness to Alexander's journey was the Greek engineer Aristobulus. He accompanied Alexander on his expedition and was responsible for numerous projects, such as the restoration of the tomb of Cyrus. His account of Alexander is uniformly positive, often to a suspicious degree. He may be forgiven his selective memory somewhat as he was in his eighties when he composed his history. Many stories of Alexander's chivalry, such as his treatment of the women in the Persian royal household, come originally from the pen of Aristobulus. He was not a soldier, but had a keen eye for geography and natural science, which is evident in Arrian's and Strabo's borrowings from his text.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[Nearchus of Crete was another childhood friend of Alexander's who accompanied him on his campaign. He is an essential source for later writers on Alexander's campaigns in India, and the best source for his own voyage as admiral of the fleet returning from the Indus to Persia.]{.style_0}

[]{#biblio.html_anchor_2967_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[Other firsthand accounts of Alexander's campaigns survived in ancient times, but their subject matter ranges from dubious anecdotes to scandalous rumors. The Greek Onesicritus was a pupil of the cynic philosopher Diogenes and helmsman on the fleet returning from India. He wrote a highly flattering account of Alexander as a philosopher-king, while his descriptions of India and the Brahmans were much used by later historians. Chares, from the Greek island of Lesbos, served as court chamberlain to Alexander in his final years. His gossipy memoir of life behind the throne took up ten books and was used by several later biographers, especially his descriptions of the]{.style_0} [proskynesis]{.style_1} [controversy and the mass marriage at Susa. A pamphlet by Ephippus, also of Olynthus, preserved several lurid tales of luxury quoted by Athenaeus. The otherwise unknown Nicobule wrote in the same vein. Medius of Thessaly is best remembered as the host of the Babylonian dinner at which Alexander's fatal decline began. He later wrote a flattering account of Alexander, perhaps to deflect charges that he had poisoned the king. Polyclitus, another Thessalian, may also have accompanied Alexander's expedition because he offers detailed geographical data quoted by Strabo. The remaining eyewitnesses who wrote of Alexander's campaign are known only by name or in brief fragments.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[Other contemporary records such as the logbooks of the expedition, the personal notebooks of Alexander, and the letters of the Macedonian leader quoted frequently by Plutarch are of questionable value at best. Some of the letters may be genuine, but others are later creations, as are the alleged logbooks and probably the notebooks as well.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[One early record of Alexander comes not from an eyewitness but from someone too young to accompany the expedition to Asia. Cleitarchus was the son of the Greek historian Dinon, who wrote a history of Persia known for its sensationalism. His son continued the family tradition with an action-packed thriller on Alexander's conquests. Written just a few years after the king's death, this multivolume work was widely read in the Greek and Roman world. Cleitarchus was able to study official accounts of the expedition during his research in Athens and Alexandria, but could also draw on the oral []{#biblio.html_anchor_2972_99}tradition from interviews with returning veterans to gain multiple perspectives of battles and other key events.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[All these earliest sources on the life of Alexander are now lost. What we do possess are the works of later historians who used them and passed their information down to us in part. One group of historians, known in modern times as the vulgate tradition, used Cleitarchus as its primary source but supplemented his work with other authors. Diodorus of Sicily wrote a forty-volume history of the world up until his lifetime in the first century B.C., which presents Alexander as a model king. Drawing on the same tradition, Diodorus' contemporary Trogus of Gaul, whose work survives only in an epitome by the third-century Latin writer Justin, more often condemns Alexander as a bloody tyrant. The Roman historian Curtius, who probably wrote during the reign of the Roman emperor Claudius, similarly criticizes Alexander in a highly rhetorical history full of invented speeches.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[The biographer Plutarch also drew on the vulgate tradition, but read widely from other sources as well. He was born in the middle of the first century A.D. in the Greek town of Chaeronea, the very place Alexander's father Philip won his decisive battle against the Greeks. As he himself admits, his aim was not to write a historical biography but rather a morally instructive life story for readers. He is generally positive in his view of Alexander, but can be critical as well. Plutarch preserves our only detailed account of Alexander's early years.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[Pride of place among Alexander's biographers, however, belongs to Arrian of Bithynia. He was born in the late first century A.D. and was educated by the famous Stoic teacher Epictetus and preserved the high moral teachings of his master in a handbook known as the]{.style_0} [Enchiridion.]{.style_1} [But Arrian was no academic recluse. He held high political office and served in the Roman army as a field commander in battles across Asia Minor. His history of Alexander is not perfect by any means, but it offers a detailed and balanced picture of a remarkable man marred by very human flaws. Arrian's primary sources were Ptolemy and Aristobulus.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[Many other Greek and Latin writers from the ancient world also mention Alexander. Strabo refers to him frequently in his]{.style_0} []{#biblio.html_anchor_2980_21}[Geography,]{.style_1} [while Athenaeus quotes many passages from lost authors in the course of his grand dinner party of philosophers. Non-Greek sources are rare, but there are a few native references to Alexander, such as Babylonian astronomical records.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[The remaining ancient evidence for Alexander is more tangible. We possess a number of valuable inscriptions from Greece and elsewhere recording decrees issued by the king or accounts of his activities. Coins issued by Alexander as payment and propaganda survive from the Mediterranean to India. Archaeology as well has revealed fascinating details about Alexander and his world. Excavations in Turkey, Iraq, Iran, Afghanistan, and of course the dazzling discoveries from the royal Macedonian tombs at Vergina in northern Greece have brought to life the world of Alexander like nothing else.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:10px;"}
:::

[**\**
]{.style_0}

[**MODERN SOURCES**]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:2px;"}
:::

[Readers wishing to explore the modern literature on Alexander have a vast array of book and articles available to them---but be aware that there are as many Alexanders as there are those who write about him.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[Political circumstances have influenced modern scholars as much as ancient authors. The work of W. W. Tarn, written during the waning days of the British Empire, remains important, though his overly positive assessment of Alexander finds little favor among scholars today. Most recent writers on Alexander provide a more mixed picture of his character, though I have read few modern scholars who seriously question his military genius.]{.style_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[For a general introduction, I highly recommend Paul Cartledge's]{.style_0} [Alexander the Great,]{.style_1} [a learned and wonderfully readable collection of studies on different stages of Alexander's life. For a gripping and insightful biography there is none better than]{.style_0} [Alexander the Great]{.style_1} [by Robin Lane Fox. Along with Fox, Peter Green's darker portrait in]{.style_0} [Alexander of Macedon]{.style_1} [should be on everyone's reading list. If you want to follow Alexander's arduous path from Greece to India and back to Babylon, you should read Michael Wood's]{.style_0} [In the Footsteps of Alexander the Great,]{.style_1} [preferably while you watch the companion PBS video.]{.style_0}

[]{#biblio.html_anchor_2991_0}

::: {style="width:100%;height:0px;"}
:::

[Just a few of the more specialized studies on Alexander that I would recommend are Waldemar Heckel's]{.style_0} [Who's Who in the Age of Alexander the Great,]{.style_1} [a useful book for keeping straight the many Persians and Macedonians who inconveniently bear the same name. Frank Holt's works on Alexander in Bactria and India are marvelous guides to the eastern campaigns, especially his]{.style_0} [Into the Land of Bones: Alexander the Great in Afghanistan.]{.style_1} [Important recent scholarship on ancient Persia includes Amélie Kuhrt's collection of primary sources in]{.style_0} [The Persian Empire,]{.style_1} [Pierre Briant's monumental study]{.style_0} [From Cyrus to Alexander,]{.style_1} [and Lindsay Allen's]{.style_0} [The Persian Empire.]{.style_1} [For the afterlife of Alexander and his legend, the books of Richard Stoneman are essential.]{.style_0}
